Positions

Source: vignettes/articles/guide-positions.Rmd
guide-positions.Rmd

A position is what a futures or options trade, or an intraday trade in shares, leaves open: a quantity you are long or short that has not been closed yet. The members on this page read this instrument’s positions and change them without being told which side you are on, so a long position is reduced by selling and a short one by buying back. Shares kept in a demat account are holdings rather than positions, and they are on Holdings. Every member on this page is defined on TradeableInstrument.

These are real orders.

The four members marked “places orders” send market or limit orders through UBI to real brokers, with real money, and none of them takes a dry_run argument. reduce_position() and liquidate_position() also let UBI choose the side, which is the point of them, so read net_positions first and be sure of what you hold. To preview one, send the same body through place_order() with dry_run = TRUE, as Under the hood shows.

The table below lists the eight members this page documents.

Kind Member Description
active binding net_positions The positions held in this instrument now, merged across every broker.
active binding day_positions Today’s own positions in this instrument, without what was carried in.
active binding positions_value What this instrument’s open positions are worth at the moment.
active binding positions_pnl What this instrument’s positions have made or lost.
places orders add_to_position() Makes an existing position bigger, or opens a new one.
places orders reduce_position() Makes an existing position smaller, without turning it around.
places orders liquidate_position() Closes one position in this instrument completely.
places orders liquidate_all_positions() Closes every position this instrument holds, under every product.

Two names for one product

UBI names a position’s product with one set of words and takes orders with another, and this is the trap on this page. A position you opened with product = "mis" comes back from net_positions with product set to intraday. The table below shows the whole mapping.

Product an order is sent with Product a position reports Can the package close it?
cnc delivery yes
mis intraday yes
nrml carry yes
none margin_trading no
none cover no
none bracket no

Every member that changes a position takes product in the order spelling, cnc, mis or nrml, and translates it. The last three rows come from order kinds UBI’s place route cannot send, such as a broker’s own bracket or cover order, so there is no order these members could write to close them. add_to_position(), reduce_position() and liquidate_position() ignore those positions entirely, as though they were not there, which means you can hold a bracket position and be told nothing is held. liquidate_all_positions() reports each one as ignored instead, with the reason, and such a position has to be closed at the broker directly. positions_value and positions_pnl count all six, because every one of them is real money.

How the side is chosen

The flowchart below shows how each of the four writing members decides which side to send. add_to_position() works the side out itself and sends a plain order. reduce_position() and liquidate_position() hand the decision to UBI, which reads the position when it sends the order.

flowchart TD
    subgraph ADD["add_to_position"]
        A1["read net_positions,<br/>keep delivery, intraday, carry"] --> A2{"anything held?"}
        A2 -- "no" --> A3{"transaction_type and<br/>product both given?"}
        A3 -- "no" --> A4["PositionError"]
        A3 -- "yes" --> A5["open a new position<br/>on the side given"]
        A2 -- "yes" --> A6{"exactly one position,<br/>or a product named<br/>that is held?"}
        A6 -- "no" --> A4
        A6 -- "yes" --> A7{"quantity above zero?"}
        A7 -- "long" --> A8["side is buy"]
        A7 -- "short" --> A9["side is sell"]
        A8 --> A10{"transaction_type given<br/>and different?"}
        A9 --> A10
        A10 -- "yes" --> A4
        A10 -- "no" --> A11["plain market or limit order,<br/>works in either mode"]
    end
    subgraph CLOSE["reduce_position and liquidate_position"]
        C1{"product named?"} -- "no" --> C2{"exactly one<br/>tradeable position?"}
        C2 -- "no" --> C3["PositionError"]
        C2 -- "yes" --> C4["use its product"]
        C1 -- "yes" --> C5{"cnc, mis or nrml?"}
        C5 -- "no" --> C3
        C5 -- "yes" --> C6["send a placeholder sell<br/>with a quantity_reference"]
        C4 --> C6
        C6 --> C7{"UBI reads the net position"}
        C7 -- "long" --> C8["UBI sends SELL"]
        C7 -- "short" --> C9["UBI sends BUY"]
        C7 -- "nothing held" --> C10["ConflictError, HTTP 409"]
    end

The practical difference between the two paths is where a mistake is caught. A missing position is a PositionError signalled here when you named no product, because the package had to read the positions to find the only one. When you named a product, nothing is read here, and a product that is not held comes back from UBI as ConflictError.

The quantity reference UBI resolves

reduce_position() and liquidate_position() send a quantity_reference, a small named list that describes the quantity instead of stating it. UBI’s order engine reads the account’s positions when it sends the order, adds up the signed quantity of every row for this instrument and product, and decides the quantity and the side from that total. The table below lists the four kinds UBI accepts; the package sends the last two.

kind Quantity sent Side sent Refused when
absolute The body’s quantity The body’s transaction_type quantity is missing or below 1
add_to_position The body’s quantity The body’s transaction_type quantity is missing or below 1
reduce_position The smaller of the body’s quantity and the position SELL for a long, BUY for a short Nothing is held (HTTP 409)
liquidate_position The whole position SELL for a long, BUY for a short Nothing is held (HTTP 409)

The reference’s optional product is spelled the positions’ way, delivery, intraday or carry, not the order way. The package translates it for you. UBI’s add_to_position kind reads no position, so it cannot choose a side, and that is why add_to_position() still works the side out in the package rather than sending a reference.

UBI’s order engine resolves the quantity reference when it sends the order, so reduce_position() and liquidate_position() need the engine running, and UBI refuses them with HTTP 503, signalled as ServiceUnavailableError, when it is not. UBI’s page on quantity references has the full rules.

Reading positions

UBI serves the whole account’s positions and has no route for one instrument, so each active binding below sends one request per access and keeps this instrument’s rows. UBI merges positions across brokers by instrument and product, so one instrument gives one row per product it is held under, and no row names a broker. Assign the result to a variable when you need it twice.

net_positions

This active binding reads GET /api/portfolio/positions. It gives the positions held in this instrument now, whenever they were opened. It is UBI’s net bucket, and it is the one every other member on this page reads.

Example

The example below prints the RELIANCE positions. When the Python version was run against a local UBI on 2026-09-26, no position was held in RELIANCE, so the property returned nothing, which in R is NULL.

reliance <- Equity$new(exchange = "nse", symbol = "RELIANCE")
print(reliance$net_positions)

Returns

The active binding gives a data.frame with one row per product held, or NULL when nothing is held in this instrument. The columns are UBI’s position fields, listed below. The fields that hold nested objects, buy, sell and pnl, are list columns, so frame$pnl[[1]][["realized"]] reads the first row’s realised profit.

Column Type Description
instrument_id character The instrument.
symbol character The symbol for a security, or the underlying for a derivative.
exchange character The exchange.
segment character The exchange-prefixed segment, such as mcx_commodity_futures.
expiry_date, strike_price, option_type character, numeric, character, or NA The contract, for a derivative.
product character delivery, intraday, carry, margin_trading, cover or bracket.
quantity numeric The net quantity in units, positive when long and negative when short.
buy, sell list column of named lists Each side’s quantity, average_price and value.
average_price numeric The average price of the open quantity.
last_price numeric or NA From the live quote when there is one, otherwise the price a broker sent.
pnl list column of named lists realized, unrealized and total, as the brokers report them.
day_change, day_change_percentage numeric or NA The change since the previous close.

Errors

The table below lists the conditions the active binding signals.

Condition When
BrokerError No broker’s positions could be read.
ServiceUnavailableError UBI’s positions document is missing or more than 30 seconds old.
UnifiedBrokerInterfaceError Any other failure reported by, or on the way to, UBI.

day_positions

This active binding reads GET /api/portfolio/positions. It gives only what was opened and closed today in this instrument, UBI’s day bucket. It has the same columns as net_positions and signals the same conditions. It is usually NULL even when net_positions is not, because only some brokers report positions on a day basis at all, so use net_positions to find out what you hold.

positions_value

This active binding reads GET /api/portfolio/positions. It says what the positions in this instrument are worth, in rupees. UBI prices a holding for you but not a position, so the package multiplies each position’s signed quantity by its last price and adds them up across products. The sign is kept: a long position adds and a short one subtracts, because a short position is an obligation to buy back. When any position has no last price, the whole answer is NULL, rather than a total quietly missing one of its parts.

Example

The example below prints the value of two instruments’ positions. In the Python version’s run on 2026-09-26, the first gave nothing, because nothing was held in RELIANCE that day, which in R is NULL. The second line assumes crude_oil_future is a CommodityFutures object holding a short position of 100 units of an MCX crude oil future with a last price of 5712.0, which is the illustrative row on UBI’s positions page; worked out from the code, it gives -571200.

print(reliance$positions_value)
print(crude_oil_future$positions_value)

Returns

The active binding gives a single numeric value in rupees, rounded to two decimal places, or NULL when nothing is held or any position has no last price. It counts positions under all six products.

Errors

It signals the same conditions as net_positions.

positions_pnl

This active binding reads GET /api/portfolio/positions. It says what the positions in this instrument have made or lost. The realised part is profit already booked by closing some of a position today, and the unrealised part is what is still riding on what remains open. Both are added across every product, and the total is worked out from the two sums.

Example

The example below prints the profit of the same illustrative crude oil position, whose row reports an unrealised profit of 1800.0 and nothing realised. Worked out from the code, the answer is a named list with realized of 0, unrealized of 1800 and total of 1800.

print(crude_oil_future$positions_pnl)

Returns

The active binding gives a named list with numeric realized, unrealized and total in rupees, each rounded to two decimal places, or NULL when nothing is held. A holding’s profit list has different names, as Holdings explains.

Errors

It signals the same conditions as net_positions.

Changing a position

The four members below place orders. price is optional on all of them: given, it sends a limit order at that price, and left out, it sends a market order, which is what closing a position usually means. The three members that close a position send that market order with synthetic = list(type = "simple", closes_position = TRUE), so the broker receives a real market order. add_to_position() sends it through buy_at_market_price() or sell_at_market_price(), which UBI runs as a limit following the other side of the book for 30 seconds, refused with HTTP 409 when that side is empty.

add_to_position

The method’s signature is shown below. It places orders: it sends GET /api/portfolio/positions, then POST /api/orders/place.

add_to_position(
  quantity,
  product = NULL,
  transaction_type = NULL,
  price = NULL,
  validity = NULL,
  after_market = FALSE,
  tag = NULL
)

This method makes an existing position bigger, or opens a new one. It reads the positions, and the direction follows the one you hold: a long position is added to by buying and a short one by selling. transaction_type is needed only when nothing is held yet, and then product is needed too, because neither can be read from a position that does not exist. A transaction_type that contradicts the position held signals PositionError and points you at reduce_position(), rather than silently reducing the position.

It sends a plain market or limit order through buy_at_market_price() and its three siblings. A limit order sent this way is held by UBI’s order engine until the book reaches its price, and a market order is sent as a marketable_limit, as Price wrappers explains.

Parameters

The table below lists the method’s parameters.

Name Type Required Default Description
quantity integer yes The quantity to add, in units and always positive, whichever way the position points.
product character or NULL no NULL The position to add to, as cnc, mis or nrml. Needed when several positions are held, and when none is.
transaction_type character or NULL no NULL buy or sell, used only to open a position when none is held.
price numeric or NULL no NULL A limit price in rupees, or NULL for a market order.
validity character or NULL no NULL day or ioc. UBI uses day when it is NULL.
after_market logical no FALSE TRUE sends an after-market order.
tag character or NULL no NULL A label of up to twenty letters and digits.

Example

The example below adds 100 units to a gold futures position, whichever way it points, and opens a new intraday short in shares where nothing is held.

gold <- CommodityFutures$new(
  exchange = "mcx",
  underlying_symbol = "GOLD",
  expiry_date = "2026-10-05"
)
gold$add_to_position(quantity = 100)

reliance <- Equity$new(exchange = "nse", symbol = "RELIANCE")
reliance$add_to_position(
  quantity = 10,
  product = "mis",
  transaction_type = "sell",
  price = 1230
)

Returns

The method returns the named list that place_order() returns.

Errors

The table below lists the conditions the method signals.

Condition When
PositionError Several positions are held and none was named, a product was named that is not held while another is, the direction given contradicts the position held, or nothing is held and transaction_type and product were not both given.
UnifiedBrokerInterfaceError Any failure reported by, or on the way to, UBI, including every condition place_order() can signal.

Opening a second product.

When a position is already held under one product, naming a different product signals PositionError rather than opening a second position, because the method only adds to what it can find. Open the second position with a price wrapper or place_order() instead.

reduce_position

The method’s signature is shown below. It places orders, and it sends POST /api/orders/place.

reduce_position(
  quantity,
  product = NULL,
  price = NULL,
  validity = NULL,
  after_market = FALSE,
  tag = NULL
)

This method makes an existing position smaller without turning it round. It sends one order carrying a reduce_position quantity reference, and UBI works out the side from the position when it sends the order: a long position is reduced by selling and a short one by buying. UBI also caps the order at what is held, so asking for more than the position closes the whole of it and never opens a new position the other way round.

When you name no product, the positions are read once here to find the only one held; when you name one, nothing is read here and UBI reads the positions itself.

Parameters

The table below lists the method’s parameters.

Name Type Required Default Description
quantity integer yes The largest quantity to close, in units and always positive.
product character or NULL no NULL The position to reduce, as cnc, mis or nrml, or NULL when only one is held.
price numeric or NULL no NULL A limit price in rupees, or NULL for a market order.
validity character or NULL no NULL day or ioc.
after_market logical no FALSE TRUE sends an after-market order.
tag character or NULL no NULL A label of up to twenty letters and digits.

Example

The example below halves an intraday futures position of 200 units, whichever way it points.

gold$reduce_position(quantity = 100, product = "mis")

Returns

The method returns the named list that place_order() returns.

Errors

The table below lists the conditions the method signals.

Condition When
PositionError No product was named and there is not exactly one tradeable position, or the product named is not cnc, mis or nrml.
ConflictError The product named is not held in this instrument, which UBI answers with HTTP 409.
ServiceUnavailableError UBI’s order engine is not running, so nothing was sent.
UnifiedBrokerInterfaceError Any other failure reported by, or on the way to, UBI.

Under the hood.

The call in the example sends the body below, worked out from the code. The transaction_type of sell is a placeholder that UBI replaces, because the route needs a side before the engine reads the reference. The synthetic list asks for UBI’s plain simple order type with closes_position set, which lets the order use the part of a broker’s daily order cap that UBI keeps for exits, so a day that used up its cap on entries can still close its positions.

{
  "instrument_id": "<the gold future's instrument_id>",
  "transaction_type": "sell",
  "order_type": "market",
  "product": "mis",
  "after_market": false,
  "dry_run": false,
  "quantity": 100,
  "quantity_reference": {"kind": "reduce_position", "product": "intraday"},
  "synthetic": {"type": "simple", "closes_position": true}
}

To preview it, send the same fields through place_order() with dry_run = TRUE, as below.

gold$place_order(
  transaction_type = "sell",
  order_type = "market",
  quantity = 100,
  product = "mis",
  dry_run = TRUE,
  quantity_reference = list(
    kind = "reduce_position",
    product = "intraday"
  ),
  synthetic = list(
    type = "simple",
    closes_position = TRUE
  )
)

liquidate_position

The method’s signature is shown below. It places orders, and it sends POST /api/orders/place.

liquidate_position(
  product = NULL,
  price = NULL,
  validity = NULL,
  after_market = FALSE,
  tag = NULL
)

This method closes one position in this instrument completely. It works exactly like reduce_position() except that it sends no quantity and a liquidate_position reference, so UBI closes the whole position, selling a long one and buying back a short one.

Parameters

The table below lists the method’s parameters.

Name Type Required Default Description
product character or NULL no NULL The position to close, as cnc, mis or nrml, or NULL when only one is held.
price numeric or NULL no NULL A limit price in rupees, or NULL for a market order.
validity character or NULL no NULL day or ioc.
after_market logical no FALSE TRUE sends an after-market order.
tag character or NULL no NULL A label of up to twenty letters and digits.

Example

The example below closes the only position held in the gold future, whatever its product and direction.

gold$liquidate_position()

Returns

The method returns the named list that place_order() returns.

Errors

It signals the same conditions as reduce_position().

liquidate_all_positions

The method’s signature is shown below. It places orders: it sends GET /api/portfolio/positions, then one POST /api/orders/place per position.

liquidate_all_positions(
  price = NULL,
  validity = NULL,
  after_market = FALSE,
  tag = NULL
)

This method closes every position this instrument holds, under every product. It reads net_positions once, then calls liquidate_position() for each tradeable product, so each close is one request that UBI sizes and directs. Every position is attempted even when an earlier one fails, and a failure is reported in the returned data frame rather than signalled. A position under margin_trading, cover or bracket is reported as ignored, with the reason, rather than passed over in silence.

It acts on this one instrument. To empty the whole account, cancelling every open order first, use Account$flatten().

Parameters

The table below lists the method’s parameters.

Name Type Required Default Description
price numeric or NULL no NULL A limit price in rupees for every order, or NULL for market orders.
validity character or NULL no NULL day or ioc.
after_market logical no FALSE TRUE sends after-market orders.
tag character or NULL no NULL A label for every order.

Example

The example below closes everything in the gold future and prints what happened. No real output is shown, because running the method closes real positions. As an illustration worked out from the code, an instrument holding a bracket position, a carried position the broker refused to close and an intraday short would give three rows in UBI’s order, which sorts by product. The bracket row would have an order_product of NA, closed set to FALSE and the error ignored: UBI cannot send a bracket order, so close this at the broker. The carry row would have an order_product of nrml, closed set to FALSE and an error naming the condition, such as OrderRejectedError: insufficient margin. The intraday row would have an order_product of mis, a quantity of -200, closed set to TRUE and the closing order’s id.

print(gold$liquidate_all_positions())

Returns

The method returns a data.frame with one row per position, or NULL when this instrument holds no position at all. The table below lists its columns.

Column Type Description
product character The position’s product, spelled the positions’ way.
order_product character or NA The product the closing order was sent with, or NA for a product UBI cannot send.
quantity numeric The signed quantity that was held.
closed logical Whether the closing order was accepted by UBI.
order_id character or NA The closing order’s id.
error character or NA Why the position was not closed.

Errors

The table below lists the conditions the method signals.

Condition When
BrokerError No broker’s positions could be read.
ServiceUnavailableError UBI’s positions document is missing or too old to serve.
UnifiedBrokerInterfaceError The positions could not be read for any other reason. A failure to close one position is reported in the data frame instead.

PositionError

PositionError is the package’s own condition for a position that cannot be changed as asked. It is signalled before anything is sent, and its class is defined with the other instrument errors in ASSETS_ERROR_PARENTS in R/assets_exceptions.R, as a child of InstrumentError, not with the UBI client’s conditions in R/unified_broker_interface_exceptions.R. The table below lists every message it carries, with <...> marking a value filled in.

Message Signalled by
No position is held in this instrument that UBI can send an order for reduce_position() and liquidate_position() with no product named
Positions are held under <products>, so name the product to act on all three, when several positions are held and no product was named
No <product> position is held in this instrument, which holds <products> add_to_position()
This is a position of <quantity> under <product>, so a <side> reduces it rather than adding to it; use reduce_position add_to_position()
No position is held in this instrument, so opening one needs both transaction_type and product add_to_position()
Positions can be closed only under cnc, mis or nrml, not '<product>' reduce_position(), liquidate_position()

Every message ends with a colon and the instrument’s description from its format() method, such as CommodityFutures(exchange='mcx', ...). The example below catches it by its class name.

tryCatch(
  gold$liquidate_position(),
  PositionError = function(error) {
    message("Nothing to close: ", conditionMessage(error))
  }
)

The Errors page lists PositionError with the rest of the package’s conditions.
